question: Should we love or hate our brother?
summary: Jesus in Luke 14:26 says no one can be his disciple unless they hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even their own life. Leviticus 19:17-18 forbids hating your brother in your heart and commands loving your neighbor as yourself, and 1 John 3:15 calls anyone who hates his brother a murderer with no eternal life in him.

reconcile.connective: Commentators uniformly read Luke's "hate" as a Semitic idiom of comparison — "love less" — so it sets priority, not literal enmity, and never cancels the command to love.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, compiler of the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses Luke 14:26 as a blunt clash with the love commands, calling the demand to hate one's family cruel and "against family values."

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: And hate not — Matthew, Mat 10:37, expresses the true meaning of this word, when he says, He who loveth his father and mother More than me. … and that this is no arbitrary interpretation of the word hate, but one agreeable to the Hebrew idiom, appears from what is said on Gen 29:30, Gen 29:31, where Leah's being hated is explained by Rachel's being loved more than Leah.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly addresses the love/hate tension: argues 'hate' in Luke 14:26 is the Hebrew idiom for 'love less,' citing Matthew's parallel and Leah/Rachel — the core harmonization.
excerpts.source_note_text: And hate not - Matthew, Mat 10:37, expresses the true meaning of this word, when he says, He who loveth his father and mother More than me. In Mat 6:24, he uses the word hate in the same sense. When we read, Rom 9:13, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated, the meaning is simply, I have loved Jacob - the Israelites, more than Esau - the Edomites; and that this is no arbitrary interpretation of the word hate, but one agreeable to the Hebrew idiom, appears from what is said on Gen 29:30, Gen 29:31, where Leah's being hated is explained by Rachel's being loved more than Leah. See also Deu 21:15-17; and Bishop Pearce on this place. See also the notes on Mat 10:37 (note).
